steps.title: Import required Node.js modules
steps.instruction: Import the http, https, and performance modules from Node.js core.
steps.hint: Use the require() function to import built-in Node.js modules. No need to install them separately.
steps.expectedOutcome: The script will have access to Node.js's HTTP, HTTPS, and performance measurement capabilities.
successCriteria: The http, https, and performance modules are imported using require().
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully imported the core modules needed for benchmarking HTTP/HTTPS endpoints.
steps.feedbackPartial: You imported some modules, but make sure to include all three: http, https, and performance.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the syntax: use require('module_name') for each built-in module.

steps.title: Define the main benchmarking function
steps.instruction: Create a function named runBenchmark that takes url and options parameters. The function should be empty for now (no implementation).
steps.hint: You can use either a function declaration or arrow function. Remember to include both parameters in parentheses.
steps.seedCode:
// Import the required modules here

// Create the runBenchmark function here
steps.expectedOutcome: A runBenchmark function is defined with url and options parameters, ready for implementation in later steps.
successCriteria: The runBenchmark function exists and accepts url and options as parameters.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully defined the main benchmarking function. This function will orchestrate all the benchmark tests.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close! Make sure your function is named exactly 'runBenchmark' and accepts both 'url' and 'options' parameters.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function definition doesn't match what's needed. Check that you've named it 'runBenchmark' and included both parameters.

steps.title: Initialize test configuration variables
steps.instruction: Inside the runBenchmark function, define three variables: requestsCount set to 100, concurrency set to 10, and results as an empty array.
steps.hint: Use const for requestsCount and concurrency, and let for results since you'll push data into it later.
steps.expectedOutcome: The runBenchmark function now has three variables initialized: requestsCount, concurrency, and results.
successCriteria: The function contains const requestsCount = 100, const concurrency = 10, and let results = [].
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the benchmark configuration variables correctly.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you have all three variables: requestsCount, concurrency, and results.
steps.feedbackWrong: Check the variable names and values. You need requestsCount = 100, concurrency = 10, and results = [].

steps.title: Create the HTTP request function
steps.instruction: Inside the runBenchmark function, create a function named makeRequest that takes a URL parameter and returns a promise that makes an HTTP GET request using the imported http module.
steps.hint: You can use the http.get method. The function should return a promise that resolves with timing data when the request completes or rejects with an error.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function is defined inside runBenchmark, returning a promise that makes HTTP requests and resolves with timing data.
successCriteria: makeRequest function exists, takes a URL parameter, returns a promise, and uses http.get to make requests.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created a reusable HTTP request function that returns a promise. This will allow us to measure individual request performance.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure makeRequest returns a promise and properly handles the HTTP request lifecycle with timing.
steps.feedbackWrong: The makeRequest function should be defined inside runBenchmark, take a URL parameter, and return a promise that makes HTTP requests.

steps.title: Implement concurrent request execution
steps.instruction: Inside the runBenchmark function, create a function named executeConcurrentRequests that uses Promise.all to run multiple requests simultaneously.
steps.hint: You can create a helper function that takes the number of concurrent requests and returns a Promise.all with an array of promises.
steps.expectedOutcome: The runBenchmark function now contains an executeConcurrentRequests function that uses Promise.all to handle concurrent requests.
successCriteria: An executeConcurrentRequests function is defined inside runBenchmark and uses Promise.all.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully implemented the concurrent request execution function using Promise.all.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've created a function, but make sure it's named executeConcurrentRequests and uses Promise.all to handle multiple requests.
steps.feedbackWrong: The function is missing or doesn't use Promise.all for concurrent execution. Try creating a function that uses Promise.all with multiple request promises.

steps.title: Add timing measurement to requests
steps.instruction: Inside the makeRequest function, add timing logic using performance.now() to measure how long each request takes, and store the duration in the results array.
steps.hint: Call performance.now() before and after the fetch request, calculate the difference, and push an object with the duration to the results array.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function will now measure and record the duration of each HTTP request.
successCriteria: The makeRequest function uses performance.now() before and after the fetch call, calculates the duration, and pushes an object with the duration to the results array.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added timing measurement to track how long each request takes.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've added some timing logic, but make sure to calculate the duration correctly and store it in the results array.
steps.feedbackWrong: The timing measurement isn't implemented correctly. Remember to use performance.now() and store the duration in the results array.

steps.title: Calculate benchmark statistics
steps.instruction: Inside the runBenchmark function, create a new function named calculateStatistics that takes the results array as a parameter and returns an object with average, min, max, and p95 response times.
steps.hint: The function should process the array of timing results to compute the required metrics. You'll need to sort the array to find the 95th percentile.
steps.expectedOutcome: The calculateStatistics function is defined inside runBenchmark and ready to process timing results.
successCriteria: A calculateStatistics function exists that takes a results array parameter and returns an object with avg, min, max, and p95 properties.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've created the statistics calculation function. This will process the timing data to give us meaningful performance metrics.
steps.feedbackPartial: You've started the function, but make sure it takes a results parameter and returns an object with all four required metrics (average, min, max, p95).
steps.feedbackWrong: The calculateStatistics function isn't properly defined. It should be a function inside runBenchmark that processes timing results and returns an object with the four metrics.

steps.title: Add error handling and retry logic
steps.instruction: Inside the makeRequest function, wrap the HTTP request logic in a try-catch block to handle errors gracefully.
steps.hint: Add try { ... } catch (error) { ... } around the existing request timing logic inside makeRequest.
steps.expectedOutcome: The makeRequest function should now have basic error handling that catches and logs request failures.
successCriteria: The makeRequest function contains a try-catch block that wraps the HTTP request logic.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've added error handling to make the benchmark more robust.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure the try-catch block properly wraps the request timing logic.
steps.feedbackWrong: The makeRequest function doesn't yet have error handling. Add a try-catch block inside it.

steps.title: Create the main script execution flow
steps.instruction: At the bottom of your file, outside the runBenchmark function, add code to call runBenchmark with example URLs and display the results.
steps.hint: Call the runBenchmark function with an array of test URLs, then use console.log to output the returned statistics.
steps.expectedOutcome: The script will be executable and will output benchmark statistics when run.
successCriteria: runBenchmark is called with an array of URLs and results are logged to the console.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've wired up the main execution flow. Your script is now ready to run benchmarks.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Make sure you're calling runBenchmark with actual URLs and logging the results.
steps.feedbackWrong: The main execution flow isn't complete. You need to call runBenchmark and display the results.

steps.title: Add command-line argument parsing
steps.instruction: At the top of your script, before the runBenchmark function, add code to parse command-line arguments using process.argv to accept URL, requests count, and concurrency as arguments.
steps.hint: process.argv is an array containing command-line arguments. The first two elements are node and the script path, so your arguments start at index 2.
steps.expectedOutcome: Your script will now accept three command-line arguments: URL, requests count, and concurrency level, making it configurable without editing the code.
successCriteria: Command-line arguments are parsed using process.argv and assigned to variables for URL, requests count, and concurrency.
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've successfully added command-line argument parsing. Your benchmark script is now configurable via command-line arguments.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track, but make sure you're parsing all three required arguments: URL, requests count, and concurrency level from process.argv.
steps.feedbackWrong: The command-line argument parsing isn't quite right. Remember to use process.argv to extract the URL, requests count, and concurrency level from the command line.
